issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of a financial corporation’s statutory recovery action is limited and does not permit a court to substitute its commercial judgment for that of the corporation.
material_facts: The borrower repeatedly defaulted on instalments, including after the corporation twice agreed to reschedule payments.
The corporation recalled the loan and took possession of the secured industrial unit under its statutory recovery powers.
The lower courts restrained the proposed sale by relying on an earlier decision without examining the relevant facts or the corporation’s conduct.
issues.conclusion: A court may interfere with the corporation’s recovery action only where it violates a statutory requirement or acts unfairly in the sense of being unreasonable; courts are not appellate authorities over its commercial decisions.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 29 and 30 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 confer recovery powers on the corporation. Under Article 226 of the Constitution, judicial review of administrative action is not an appeal on the merits: intervention is warranted for statutory violation or unreasonable unfairness, not merely because a court prefers a different commercial decision. The Court relied on U.P. Financial Corporation v. Gem Cap (India) Pvt. Ltd., U.P. Financial Corporation v. Naini Oxygen & Acetylene Gas Ltd., Karnataka State Financial Corporation v. Micro Cast Rubber & Allied Products (P) Ltd., A.K. Kraipak v. Union of India, Secretary of State for Education and Science v. Metropolitan Borough Council of Tameside, and Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation.

predicates.challenge_to_statutory_lender_recovery: A party asks a court to review a financial lender’s exercise of statutory recovery powers.
predicates.statutory_noncompliance: The lender’s recovery action fails to comply with a statutory requirement.
predicates.arbitrary_unreasonable_action: The lender acts so unfairly or unreasonably that no reasonable decision-maker would have acted that way.

issues.definition: When statutory lender recovery is challenged, intervention is justified if the action is legally noncompliant or arbitrary and unreasonable.

issues.legal_issue: A financial corporation’s statutory power to enforce its security is not subject to mandatory borrower consultation at every stage of the sale process.
material_facts: The borrower defaulted repeatedly despite two accepted requests to reschedule instalments.
The corporation took possession of the secured unit and sought to sell it to recover the debt.
An earlier decision had prescribed detailed sale guidelines requiring the borrower’s involvement at stages of the sale.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decision’s guidelines imposing those restrictions on the corporation’s recovery power were contrary to the letter and intent of the statute and did not state the correct law; that decision was overruled.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29(1) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 permits a corporation, upon default, to take over management or possession and deal with the secured property. The Court held that the guidelines in Mahesh Chandra v. Regional Manager, U.P. Financial Corporation unnecessarily restricted that power and conflicted with the approach in U.P. Financial Corporation v. Gem Cap (India) Pvt. Ltd., U.P. Financial Corporation v. Naini Oxygen & Acetylene Gas Ltd., and Karnataka State Financial Corporation v. Micro Cast Rubber & Allied Products (P) Ltd.

predicates.statutory_lender_realizes_secured_indust: A statutory financial lender seeks to realize assets secured for an industrial loan.
predicates.borrower_is_in_default: The borrower has failed to meet repayment or other obligations owed to the lender.

issues.definition: When a statutory lender realizes secured industrial assets after default, the borrower need not be consulted as a mandatory precondition to sale.

issues.legal_issue: A sale of seized assets should use a transparent process that encourages competition and seeks the best obtainable price, with appropriate publicity.
material_facts: The corporation had taken possession of an industrial unit securing an unpaid loan and contemplated its disposal.
The Court considered the need to recover public funds while ensuring that disposal of the seized unit obtained the highest price.
issues.conclusion: The corporation must use a transparent and acceptable disposal procedure intended to realize the highest price, with due publicity wherever possible; public auction is generally effective, but another suitable method may be used where an auction is unsuitable or unlikely to secure the best price.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 authorizes realization of secured property. In considering disposal of public property, the Court relied on The Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd., which explains that public auction after adequate publicity generally promotes participation and the best price, while tenders or another suitable method may be appropriate in some circumstances if adequate publicity is given.

predicates.seized_asset_is_to_be_sold: A lender is disposing of an asset it has seized to recover a debt.
predicates.sale_process_can_be_made_competitive: The disposal can be conducted through a process that allows interested purchasers a fair opportunity to participate.
predicates.best_price_is_the_disposal_objective: The seller seeks to obtain the highest price reasonably available for the asset.

issues.definition: If a seized asset is being sold through a process capable of inviting competition to obtain the best price, the sale must be transparent and directed toward the highest price.

issues.legal_issue: A court must apply precedent in the context of the facts and issue it decided rather than treating judicial observations as statutory rules.
material_facts: The lower courts relied on an earlier decision to restrain the sale without addressing how its factual setting matched this case.
The earlier decision’s broad guidelines had been expressed without accounting for the statutory purpose and practical circumstances relevant to the present recovery action.
issues.conclusion: Courts must examine the factual fit of a precedent and read judicial observations in context; decisions cannot be applied mechanically as though their words were statutory provisions.
issues.legal_principle: Judgments are to be understood in the setting of their facts, and even a significant factual difference may change the result. The Court relied on London Graving Dock Co. Ltd. v. Horton, Home Office v. Dorset Yacht Co., Herrington v. British Railways Board, and the principle stated by Lord Denning that precedent should be followed only so far as it serves the path of justice.

predicates.court_relies_on_prior_judgment: A court uses an earlier judgment as a basis for deciding the dispute before it.
predicates.material_factual_fit_is_not_examined: The court does not assess whether the facts and issue of the earlier judgment correspond to the case being decided.

issues.definition: A court relying on an earlier judgment without examining its factual fit must not apply that judgment mechanically.

issues.legal_issue: A financial corporation is not required to keep financing or reviving every defaulting industrial unit, and a borrower seeking indulgence must establish genuine circumstances preventing repayment.
material_facts: The corporation lent public funds for the purpose of supporting industrial activity and needed repayments to provide assistance to other borrowers.
The borrower repeatedly failed to pay despite rescheduling and had repaid no material portion of the principal.
The borrower did not establish that insurmountable difficulties prevented repayment or that it had a genuine intention to repay.
issues.conclusion: The corporation’s duty to act fairly does not disable it from recovering amounts due or require it to continue supporting a chronic defaulter; a borrower claiming inability to meet commitments because of exceptional difficulties must establish those circumstances with material.
issues.legal_principle: The State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 was enacted to promote industrialization through loans repayable within a stipulated period. A corporation is a creditor, not a trustee or business partner of the borrower, and must recover funds to lend them again. U.P. Financial Corporation v. Gem Cap (India) Pvt. Ltd. supports the principle that promoting industry does not justify putting public funds into a unit without regard to the cost or prospect of recovery.

predicates.public_financial_lender_has_advanced_rep: A public financial lender has provided funds on terms requiring repayment.
predicates.borrower_has_repeatedly_defaulted: The borrower has repeatedly failed to make required payments, including after opportunities to reschedule them.
predicates.borrower_proves_genuine_preventing_diffi: The borrower provides material establishing genuine, exceptional circumstances that prevented repayment despite an intention to meet its commitments.

issues.definition: A public lender that has advanced repayable funds and faces repeated default need not continue indulgence or finance revival unless the borrower establishes genuine preventing difficulties.

issues.legal_issue: A borrower who offers to repay after persistent default may be given a conditional final opportunity, with disposal of the secured unit remaining available if repayment is not made.
material_facts: The borrower had repeatedly defaulted despite rescheduling and had not repaid a material portion of the principal.
During the appeal, the borrower stated that it would try to pay the amount due if given reasonable time.
The corporation opposed the request, but the Court granted a conditional opportunity to test the borrower’s bona fides.
issues.conclusion: The corporation was directed to inform the borrower of the amount due, and the borrower was allowed a final period to pay it in full; if payment was not made, the corporation could dispose of the seized unit according to law in a manner intended to obtain the highest price. The appeal was allowed to that extent.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion in the particular circumstances while maintaining the corporation’s statutory recovery rights under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951. The opportunity was conditional, and failure to pay left the corporation free to dispose of the unit in accordance with law.

predicates.appeal_challenges_injunction_against_sei: An appeal concerns an injunction restraining a statutory lender from selling an asset it has seized.
predicates.borrower_has_repeatedly_defaulted: The borrower has repeatedly failed to pay amounts due despite earlier repayment accommodations.
predicates.borrower_offers_to_repay_if_given_time: The borrower offers to pay the amount due if given additional time.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning an injunction against sale, a repeatedly defaulting borrower’s offer to repay may support a conditional opportunity to pay before sale.
